sources.name: CWE catalogue entries examined by hand for a pure-Perl bit-validation library. No Perl-specific MITRE view is known to this review (MITRE publishes language views for C, C++ and Java, among others), so no view id is cited and no member-list snapshot exists; the considered_not_included list is a reviewer list, not a view walk (VER15a section 9 rule 9 cannot be checked for this lane)

Perl language pitfalls: scalars are strings and numbers at once (numification, "0 but true", inf/nan strings, dualvars via Scalar::Util), == versus eq, truthiness of "0.0", undef and warnings, references and overload, tie, local $@ and die with objects, string eval and symbolic references, AUTOLOAD and glob assignment, context sensitivity, regex backtracking, IV/UV/NV promotion, CPAN install model (perlop, perldata, perlsub, overload, perltie, perlre, Scalar::Util)
LG02 sections 7 and 9: error identity and the type-confusion matrix (perl row and lane-specific rows)

This repo's audits of the perl lane: LGE-P1 (PR #19927, merged: four security-review rounds found numeric-!= validation, dualvars computed on the numeric part, invocant guessing that dropped inputs, unbounded widths), LGE-ID-perl (PR #19944, merged: Error class), and by-hand probes of origin/main fb9d1d3d37e on perl 5.34.1 recorded in the threat rationales (ShiftRegister state elements and serial_out, scalar-context returns, tied scalar fetch count, ANDn timing)

implementations: perl as installed by the CI image or the developer machine (BUILD:3, BUILD_windows:3); probes for this review ran on perl 5.34.1 (darwin-thread-multi-2level); no second interpreter or version is exercised

threats.name: Use After Free
threats.rationale: Perl manages memory itself (reference-counted scalars, arrays and hashes; indexing past the end yields undef), so a pure-Perl package cannot reach this class unless it loads native code. The library loads none by reading (LogicGates.pm:58-64, :89-91; Error.pm:39-47), and the sibling Transistors distribution is pure Perl. The exclusion needs an analyzer rule that proves "no XS, Inline or FFI, no raw-pointer pack template" for the package and its dependencies; none exists. Perl analogue worth naming: reading $a[$n] past the end returns undef with a warning, which the gates then reject as undef (matrix row, t/02-validation.t:58-88), not a stray read.

closed_by.detail: No XSLoader, DynaLoader, Inline::*, FFI::Platypus, FFI::Raw, Win32::API, B, Devel::Peek, syscall, and no pack/unpack/vec template that handles raw pointers (p, P) in the library or in a transitive CPAN dependency. By reading, LogicGates.pm imports only strict, warnings, Scalar::Util, Exporter, constant, overload, its own Error class and CodingAdventures::Transistors (LogicGates.pm:58-64, :89-91; Error.pm:39-41, :47); the Transistors distribution ships no .xs file. Scalar::Util, Exporter, overload and constant are core modules of the interpreter itself (Scalar::Util is XS inside perl) and are part of the trusted runtime base, not of this package. No Perl analyzer exists: ca-capability-analyzer is merged for go, ocaml, python, rust and typescript only (code/packages/*/ca-capability-analyzer); the Perl rule table is LGE-A1 and its wiring into the report is LGE-W1.

threats.name: NULL Pointer Dereference
threats.rationale: Perl has no null pointers, but its analogue is dereferencing undef or a non-reference: under use strict a string used as a HASH reference dies with a plain Perl message, and an rvalue $x->{k} on an undef element AUTOVIVIFIES the element into a hash in the caller's data. The gates validate every scalar before use, but ShiftRegister reads $_->{slave_q} from every element of the caller's state array BEFORE validating the elements (LogicGates.pm:916). Probe on perl 5.34.1: ShiftRegister(1,1,[0],"left") and (…,["x"],…) die with "Can't use string (...) as a HASH ref while strict refs" and ([[]]) with "Not a HASH reference" (plain strings, not Error objects), and ShiftRegister(1,1,[undef],"left") turns the caller's undef element into {} before dying. No memory is corrupted, so the memory-safety exclusion (gc_runtimes) holds with the native-code rule, but the identity and mutation defects are real and are recorded in perl.state-element-validation and perl.exception-identity.

threats.name: Integer Overflow to Buffer Boundary
threats.rationale: The narrow class (wraparound that sizes a buffer). Perl integers promote silently from IV to UV to NV (no wraparound, no undefined behaviour), and the counts that size anything are the validated Counter width (at most 65536, matching /\A[1-9][0-9]{0,4}\z/, LogicGates.pm:664, :672, so `(0) x $width` at :679 and :982 cannot be absurd) and array lengths taken with scalar @{...} (:861), which on main are NOT capped for ANDn, ORn, XORn, Register and ShiftRegister (perl.nary-and-container-length-unbounded); those are caller-owned arrays, not a computed size that wraps. Not a statement about integer overflow in general, which Perl does not have in the C sense.

threats.name: OS Command Injection
threats.rationale: A gate package is pure computation: it takes bits and returns bits and the library imports no file, process, network, database, UI or serialization module (LogicGates.pm:58-64, :89-91; Error.pm:39-47). Exclusion needs an analyzer rule that checks that for the sources and their dependencies; none exists for Perl, and the package has no required_capabilities.json at all (sibling Perl packages do), so nothing even declares the empty set. Perl-specific shapes this excludes: backticks, qx, system, exec, two-argument open with a pipe, and a pipe open on a caller value; the library has none.

threats.rationale: Perl's regex engine backtracks, so ReDoS is possible for a pattern with nested quantifiers on attacker text. threats.name: Tied scalars, arrays and hashes, and other magic that runs caller code on every read

threats.name: Exception identity: die with an object, $@ clobbering, hooks, plain-string dies
threats.rationale: Callers must be able to tell WHY a call died without matching text. threats.name: Error text built from caller data: format strings, log injection, disclosure
threats.rationale: Messages are the usual carrier of a format-string or log-injection bug. Here every message is a literal with the caller value inserted through _describe: undef, a reference named by type, or the first 32 characters with each non-printable replaced by \xNN, cut before copying so a 10 MB string costs 32 characters (LogicGates.pm:162-173); the only sprintf has the constant format '\x%02x' (:171) and a % in a rejected value is printed literally (probe: "%s%n%d" gives "got '%s%n%d'"). Up to 32 characters of a rejected value reach the message, so a caller that passes a secret as a "bit" discloses 32 characters of it into whatever logs the exception. The error object keeps only the bounded rendering, never the raw value (Error.pm:31-34).

closed_by.detail: _describe cuts the value to 32 characters before copying, escapes every non-printable as \xNN and never interpolates a reference or calls an overload (LogicGates.pm:162-173). t/02-validation.t:138-140 (reference named by type, control characters escaped, long value truncated) and :367-374 (a 10 MB string gives an error under 200 bytes for AND and for new_counter_state), :446-451 (value_description bounded).

No sprintf, printf, warn, die or Carp call whose format string or first message argument is built from caller data. By reading the one sprintf has the constant format '\\x%02x' with the character code as argument (LogicGates.pm:171) and every die goes through _throw with a literal message plus the bounded rendering from _describe (:68-72, :182). No Perl analyzer exists: ca-capability-analyzer is merged for go, ocaml, python, rust and typescript only (code/packages/*/ca-capability-analyzer); the Perl rule table is LGE-A1 and its wiring into the report is LGE-W1.

threats.name: Late-bound subs: any code can redefine a package function or an imported builtin wrapper
threats.rationale: Perl resolves a sub by name in the package symbol table at call time, so any code in the process can replace what the library calls: *CodingAdventures::LogicGates::_is_bit = sub { 1 } (under no warnings "redefine"), local *CodingAdventures::LogicGates::cmos_and, *Scalar::Util::reftype, or *CORE::GLOBAL::die. The helper subs and the imported cmos_* functions are looked up through the stash on every call (LogicGates.pm:89, :153, :178). A caller that can do that already has arbitrary code execution in the process, so this is outside what a package can prevent; it is stated so a report does not read "validated" as "tamper-proof".

threats.name: Memory allocation sized by a caller number (counter width)
threats.rationale: new_counter_state(width) and Counter(clock, reset, state) allocate and loop over `width` bits, where width is a caller number. The check is a strict string pattern (1 to 5 digits, no leading zero) and a cap of MAX_WIDTH 65536, applied to the string form before any allocation or arithmetic (LogicGates.pm:661-673), so a reference (which numifies to an address of about 1e11), 1e12, "999999999999", 2**40, Inf and 65537 are rejected before `(0) x $width` runs (t/02-validation.t:332-345). The Counter's own bits array must have exactly `width` elements (:977-978). Other caller-chosen lengths are in perl.nary-and-container-length-unbounded.

threats.name: Caller-chosen list lengths with no cap (ANDn, ORn, XORn, Register, ShiftRegister)
threats.rationale: The variadic gates, Register and ShiftRegister take a list or array whose length the caller chooses and process it with no limit: ANDn/ORn/XORn copy it (LogicGates.pm:510-512, :516) and call a validated gate once per element, Register builds a flip-flop per element and runs every DFlipFlop (:861-879), ShiftRegister does the same (:913-940). Probe on perl 5.34.1: ANDn over 300000 ones took about 6 s. The Go, Python and Haskell lanes had the same defect and got caps (LGE-DOS-ALL); Perl has none. A cap needs the code change and a bound test, which do not exist.

closed_by.detail: A test that ANDn, ORn, XORn, Register and ShiftRegister reject more than MAX_WIDTH (65536) inputs or elements with INVALID_ARITY or INVALID_SHAPE before looping, and still accept exactly MAX_WIDTH. Per-function limits are needed, not one shared 65536 (see build-check:perl.bounded-step-and-cpu-benchmark). Today none is capped: a probe on perl 5.34.1 ran ANDn over 300000 ones in about 6 s, so 1e6 inputs is about 20 s of CPU and a caller-chosen array is also copied twice (LogicGates.pm:510-512, :516).

threats.name: Method-versus-function guessing and argument dropping
threats.rationale: Perl subs receive a flat @_, so a function that guessed "method call" from a leading package name or from the argument count silently dropped an input: before PR #19927, ANDn("CodingAdventures::LogicGates", 1, 1) returned 1 and AND(x, y, z) dropped x. The fix makes every public function a plain function: _args only counts arguments (LogicGates.pm:209-218), a leading package name is ordinary data that fails validation or arity, and Class->AND(1, 1) dies with an arity error. Arity is checked for every function (INVALID_ARITY). New code could reintroduce guessing; no rule forbids shift-and-compare on @_[0].

closed_by.detail: Public functions are plain functions that never guess a method call: _args only counts arguments (LogicGates.pm:209-218). t/02-validation.t:146-156 (arity of AND, NOT, XOR, leading package name not stripped) and :381-414 (every public function, including Class->AND, rejects a leading package name as data or by arity).

threats.name: Context-sensitive return values (list returned in scalar context)
threats.rationale: Perl subs return different things in list and scalar context. SRLatch, DLatch, DFlipFlop, Register, ShiftRegister and Counter return lists (LogicGates.pm:734, :836, :878, :929, :940, :1001), and `my $q = SRLatch(...)` evaluates the comma operator and yields only the LAST element, q_bar, with no error: the caller receives the complement of what they wanted. The gates return one scalar and are not affected. Nothing in the package tests or guards the scalar-context call.

closed_by.detail: A test (and a wantarray check in the code) that SRLatch, DLatch, DFlipFlop, Register, ShiftRegister and Counter, which return lists, die with a typed error when called in scalar context instead of returning only their last element (`my $q = SRLatch(...)` yields q_bar today, the comma operator, LogicGates.pm:734).

threats.name: Behaviour that depends on warnings: -w, no warnings, FATAL warnings, __WARN__ hooks
threats.rationale: In Perl the numeric-conversion mistakes are warnings, not errors, and the effective setting is lexical and can be flipped by the caller (`no warnings`, `use warnings FATAL => "all"`, -w, a $SIG{__WARN__} that dies). A validator that relied on a warning, or that emitted one, would behave differently per caller. The string-form check uses no numeric operator on an unvalidated value, so its outcome is warning-independent; the matrix collects warnings and asserts none, and repeats AND under FATAL warnings (t/02-validation.t:98-125). The library itself uses plain use warnings (LogicGates.pm:59).

threats.name: Unicode digits and wide characters that look or numify like 0 and 1
threats.rationale: Perl strings are sequences of code points, so "\x{FF11}" (fullwidth one), "\x{661}" (Arabic-Indic one) and "1\0" are different from "1". The check is an ASCII character class anchored with \A and \z, not \d (which matches any Unicode digit under /u), so these are rejected by reading (LogicGates.pm:157); the escape step prints them as \x{...}-style codes (:171, probe: "\x263a" for a smiley). None of these values is in the matrix.

closed_by.detail: The LG02 section 9 rows the suite lacks (t/02-validation.t:58-88): wide integers 256, 2**32, 2**32+1, 2**53+1, 2**64, 1e100 and negatives; "0x1", "1e0", "1_0", "0e0"; fullwidth and Arabic-Indic digits ("\x{FF11}", "\x{661}"); "1\0"; computed -0.0; !!0; a tied scalar; a nested array [[1]]; a glob and a filehandle; a qr// object; and, in every gate, a bad value in the SECOND position with the first argument 0 (the matrix only ever holds the other argument at 1, t/02-validation.t:93-96), which is the short-circuit row.

LogicGates.pm:153-158 (_is_bit: defined, not a reference, string form matches /\A[01]\z/) and :178-191 (_bit returns a fresh IV 0 or 1 computed from the string form) run before any numeric operator touches a value; the check never uses a numeric operator on unvalidated input, so it behaves the same under -w, no warnings and FATAL warnings. A runtime guard exercised by the suite, not a language guarantee: Perl enforces no type at the call boundary.

threats.name: Results that vary by perl version, build or platform
